sections.content: How exposed are mortgage holders and renters in Solihull to rising housing costs?
In total, 33.1% of all households in Solihull were owned with a mortgage and 12.8% were rented privately, according to Census 2021 data.

sections.content:
Mortgage holders in Solihull are at high exposure to rising housing costs

An estimated 16.3% of all households in Solihull experienced rising mortgage costs in 2023. This is one of the highest of all areas in England and Wales.

Those in Solihull whose mortgage costs rose are estimated to have seen an average increase of £202 a month, from £934 in 2022 to £1,135 in 2023.

This rise is higher than the average in England and Wales, and is equivalent to 6.4% of disposable income for an average household.

After this rise, new housing costs for affected mortgage holders would be around 35.8% of the average disposable income in Solihull. This is higher than the average in England and Wales.

Combined, these measures give Solihull a high overall exposure score for mortgage holders of 6 out of 7.

sections.content:
Rising costs have not impacted mortgage holders equally in Solihull.

The amount it costs to remortgage depends on several factors, including:

  • interest rates at the time
  • loan to value ratio
  • outstanding mortgage amount
  • the remaining term.

For example, a household coming off a five-year fixed-rate mortgage in January 2023 would have seen a lower than average cost increase, at an estimated £119. This would equate to around 3.8% of average household disposable income.

Those coming off a two-year fixed-rate mortgage in November 2023 would have seen higher than average rises in their monthly repayments, increasing by an estimated £320, or 10.1% of average household disposable income.

Exposure to rising mortgages was more likely in areas with higher house prices and less likely in areas with a high number of retirees, or homes owned outright.

Average house prices in Solihull were £328,000 in 2022, which is higher than the average across England and Wales of £283,000.

Mortgage-holders who may be the most protected from rising costs are those who have a lower loan amount, including those who bought when prices were lower or have had more time to pay off their mortgage.

Households headed by older people are more likely to have paid off more of their mortgage and be less exposed to rising housing costs.

In Solihull, 30.2% of all households were headed were retirees according to Census 2021 data, which is higher than the average of all areas in England and Wales.

sections.content:
Renters in Solihull are at medium exposure to rising housing costs

Among those in Solihull who experienced rising private rents, the average estimated increase was £103, rising from £988 in 2022 to £1,091 in 2023.

This rise is one of the highest in England and Wales, and is equivalent to 3.2% of disposable income for an average household in Solihull.

After this rise, new housing costs for affected renters would be around 34.4% of the average disposable income in Solihull. This is higher than the average in England and Wales.

Rent rises affected an estimated 6.4% of all households in Solihull in 2023. This is one of the lowest of all areas in England and Wales.

Combined, these measures give Solihull a medium overall exposure score for renters of 4 out of 7.

sections.content:
In general, areas with more students or overcrowded housing are more likely to have a high proportion of renters, and so are more likely to be exposed to rising rents.

The proportion of student households in Solihull was 0.3% according to Census 2021 data, which is one of the lowest in England and Wales.

Solihull also has similar to the average proportions of overcrowded homes, at 2.6% of all households.

Private rent rises in Solihull were more common among three bedroom properties, at 38.6% of affected households.

Among affected households, average private rent rises ranged from £61 for a one bedroom property to £132 for a four bedroom property.

sections.content:
How does Solihull compare with the rest of the West Midlands?

So far we have been comparing housing costs in Solihull to all areas in England and Wales, which can conceal more localised effects.

It can be useful to focus on how housing costs are changing relative to the rest of the West Midlands.

The most common exposure scores in the West Midlands were 2 for mortgages and 3 for rents.

This means households in Solihull are more exposed for mortgages and more exposed for rents than most other areas in the West Midlands.

Within the West Midlands, 14.0% of households are estimated to have seen mortgage costs rise, and 9.0% estimated to have seen private rents rise.

In comparison, Solihull has a higher proportion of households affected by mortgage rises and a lower proportion of households affected by rent rises.

Among affected households in the West Midlands, mortgage costs rose by an average of £148 and private rents rose by an average of £79.

Cost rises for those affected in Solihull were higher for mortgages and higher for rents.

Which areas have similar exposure scores to Solihull ?

We can dig a little deeper to see which areas have similar exposure scores to Solihull, and why that might be.

There are eight local authorities in England and Wales with the same exposure scores as Solihull for both renters and mortgage holders.

They include Central Bedfordshire, Wealden, Castle Point, Chelmsford and Basingstoke and Deane.

We can explore whether these areas tend to be similar to Solihull in other ways, using newly published clustering analysis.

Areas with populations which share similar characteristics are in the same "demographic cluster", and those with similar economy activity are in the same "economic cluster".

Matching on either of these clusters could indicate a relationship between exposure to housing costs and factors like age, income, house prices or economic activity.

Most of the areas with similar exposure scores to Solihull are also either economically or demographically similar.

sections.title: How do places with the same exposure scores as Solihull  compare economically and demographically?
sections.footer: Source: Office for National Statistics – Who has been affected by changing housing costs across England and Wales

sections.content:
In general, Solihull is among a group of areas which tend to have higher than average house prices, productivity and employment, with moderately high disposable income.

This is similar to Wealden.

Solihull is in a cluster of areas which tend to have a large under-16 population and fast population growth.

This is similar to Central Bedfordshire.

There are four areas which are similar both economically and demographically and have the same exposure scores to Solihull. These are Chelmsford, Basingstoke and Deane, Mid Sussex and Trafford.

sections.content:
The picture across England and Wales

London is particularly affected by rising rents, largely because it has a high proportion of renters and pre-existing high rents.

Of all households in London, 23.1% are estimated to have seen rents rise, which is the highest in England and Wales.

Rents rose for 12.9% of households in England as a whole, and 7.0% of households in Wales.

Those affected in London saw the highest average monthly rent increase of £175 (9.9%), from £1,764 to £1,939.

This compares to the North East, where affected households saw the smallest rent rises of £63 (10.5%), from £601 to £664.

Across England as a whole average rents for affected households rose by 9.7%, from £1,129 to £1,238, and by 11.3% in Wales, from £635 to £707.

Overall, London boroughs are some of the most exposed to rising rents, with 96.9% assigned the highest exposure score of 7.

sections.content:
Mortgage payment rises in 2023 are also estimated to be higher in London, rising by £458 (30.6%), from £1,496 to £1,954.

In comparison, households in the rest of England saw mortgage costs rise by £178 (21.7%), from £821 to £999, while for those in Wales they rose by £120 (21.8%), from £551 to £670.

While mortgage costs were highest in London, they affected the smallest proportion of households.

Around 12.1% of households in London were affected by rising mortgages, compared with 15.5% in the South East and 15.1% in the East of England.

Local authorities in these regions had some of the highest exposure scores for rents as a result. The most common exposure score for rents in these local authorities was a 6.

sections.title: Areas with the lowest exposure to mortgage or rent increases tended to be in the North of England and Wales
sections.subtitle: Local authorities in England and Wales that had exposure scores of 2 and below for renters or mortgage holders in 2023
sections.footer: Source: Office for National Statistics – Who has been affected by changing housing costs across England and Wales

sections.content:
Overall, areas with the lowest exposure to rising housing costs were in the North East.

Around 3 in every 4 local authorities in the North East had a low rent exposure score. More than half (58.3%) were assigned a low score of 2, and 16.7% had the lowest score of 1.

Among these local authorities, the average rise in rents was £63, affecting 8.1% of households.

Half of all local authorities in the North East had a mortgage exposure score of 2, and 8.3% had a score of 1.

The average rise in monthly mortgage payments in the North East was £110, affecting 13.7% of households.
